report:
**Conclusion: the claim is true, not false.** Strong randomized-trial evidence shows that the adjuvanted recombinant zoster vaccine (RZV; Shingrix) substantially reduces shingles in adults aged **70 years or older**.

The key evidence is ZOE-70, an international, phase-3, randomized, observer-blind, placebo-controlled trial. It enrolled 13,900 adults aged ≥70 (6,950 assigned vaccine and 6,950 placebo), with two doses given two months apart. The peer-reviewed trial concluded that the glycoprotein-E subunit vaccine reduced both herpes zoster and postherpetic neuralgia in this age group. Reported vaccine efficacy against shingles was approximately **91%** over a median follow-up of about four years—meaning a large relative reduction, though not complete prevention.

This is not solely an inference from a younger population: ZOE-70 specifically studied the requested age group. FDA labeling likewise describes the pivotal placebo-controlled trial in adults ≥70. Real-world evidence in adults ≥50 from four US health systems also found high effectiveness, supporting that trial findings translate outside tightly controlled studies, although that observational study is less specific to ≥70.

Important qualifications: the finding applies to the **two-dose** recombinant, adjuvanted vaccine; it does not mean every recipient is protected indefinitely, nor does it establish identical benefit for every frail or highly comorbid subgroup. But those limitations do not support the view that RZV fails to reduce shingles in people ≥70.
